newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: EU makes political push on China's WTO membership.
newsitem.headline: EU makes political push on China's WTO membership.

text.p: The European Union launched a political drive on Tuesday to breathe new life into long-running talks over China's bid to join the World Trade Organisation.

Delegates from the Quad -- the United States, Japan, Canada and the EU -- met for lunch at the initiative of European Trade Commisioner Sir Leon Brittan to take stock of prospects for resuming serious negotiations over Beijing's accession bid.

EU officials said Brittan, who negotiates on trade issues on behalf of the 15 EU members, had been encouraged to sound out the Quad after receiving positive political signals during a recent visit to Beijing.

"What we're looking to do is to get over some of the political hesitations and the political logjam that has slowed the negotiations down to stalling point in the last 18 months," Peter Guilford, Brittan's spokesman, told reporters.
"We've got to get the political message across now that the talks should begin again. Then we've got to agree the right terms," he added.
Guilford said Brittan wanted to gauge the level of support within the Quad for the concept of a phased approach to China's membership of the 128-strong world trade body.
Washington, by contrast, insists that Beijing comply with a "road map" to open its markets and eliminate trade and non-trade barriers before it can win U.S. support for its entry.
Guilford stressed that breakthroughs were unlikely at Singapore.
"It's a bit hasty to say that this Quad... is going to iron out most of the issues relating to the fastest-developing and biggest developing country in the world joining the WTO.
"We'd like that to happen but even our own optimism doesn't stretch that far," he said.
Brittan believes WTO membership would help to lock in China's market reforms but has made it clear to Beijing's top economic officials that the entrance fee would be high.

The Brussels-based Commission, the EU's executive arm, has suggested that a downpayment by China on joining the WTO might include a serious tariff-cutting offer, an end to the state's virtual monopoly on external trade and tighter protection of intellectual property.
Other obligations, and matching benefits, would then be phased in gradually.

"Clearly, once we begin negotiating again in earnest with the Chinese, it will be an extremely difficult, arduous, highly detailed negotiation -- nobody is pretending it's going to be easy," Guilford said.

"Nor does our political enthusiasm for this mean that we are going to go easy on the details," he added. "We and the United States agree that China should come in as soon as possible but on the right terms."
China had hoped to culminate its decade-long bid to join the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade by becoming a founding member of the WTO when it replaced the GATT two years ago.
Its application foundered on opposition over entry terms, with Beijing maintaining that demands made of it were too stiff.

Senior Chinese analyst Pei Changhong said last week China was unlikely to concede on its demand to enter the WTO as a developing country and has the patience to hunker down for a long wait to win accession on its terms.
The United States insists that the size of China's economy ranks it as a developed country.
A goal of 1997 entry seemed an ambitious target given the distance between the United States and China on so many issues, but Pei said he hoped to see entry by 1999.
